strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important gap: efficient, numerically tight privacy loss accounting for random allocation (used in DP-SGD variants such as balls-and-bins/PREAMBLE), improving substantially over prior RDP/hockey-stick approximations from Feldman & Shenfeld (2025) and Dong et al. (2025), which incur up to ~20-60% looseness in epsilon.

Clean and non-trivial theoretical contribution: the notion of PLD realization and the characterization of the random-allocation PLD as a (t-wise) convolution of exponentiated PLDs (exp-PLDs) and their PLD duals is an elegant reduction that enables efficient, provably tight numerical computation (Theorem 4.4, 4.6).

Rigorous complexity analysis (O(log^3(t) log(t/beta)/alpha^2)) with matching stochastic-domination-based tightness guarantees (alpha, beta), including both upper and lower bounds, which is unusual rigor for this line of empirical PLD-accounting work.

Strong empirical validation: numerical bounds nearly match Monte Carlo simulation results and known lower bounds (Fig. 1, 2, 6), and the method is shown practical (seconds to tens of seconds) across realistic parameter regimes (Fig. 3).

Broader methodological contribution beyond random allocation: shows how to perform Poisson subsampling directly on PLD realizations (Theorem 3.3), generalizing accurate accounting beyond composition to any dominated algorithm, not just Gaussian/Laplace mechanisms as in current libraries.

Demonstrates real practical impact by improving privacy accounting for the PREAMBLE communication-efficient DP-SGD algorithm (Asi et al., 2025), showing meaningfully tighter noise-vs-privacy tradeoffs than RDP-based accounting used in the original work (Fig. 5).

Thorough treatment of implementation details (full pseudocode in Appendix C), numerical stability considerations, and comparison between FFT-based and direct multiplicative convolution approaches, aiding reproducibility; code is released.
weaknesses: No new utility/accuracy experiments beyond a single toy mean-estimation replication (Fig. 4); the paper explicitly defers to prior work for utility claims, which is reasonable given the privacy-accounting focus but means the paper's practical value proposition ("random allocation now provably beats Poisson for DP-SGD utility") rests partly on combining this paper's bounds with separate, previously published utility results rather than a unified empirical demonstration.

The paper is extremely dense with heavy notation, multiple domination/duality notions (hockey-stick domination, stochastic domination, PLD duals, exp-PLD transforms), and deferred proofs, which may limit accessibility and reproducibility for readers not already steeped in the PLD-accounting literature; the main text is largely a technical overview with most substance in the appendix.

The FFT-based convolution alternative is presented without formal tightness/error guarantees (only empirical validity), leaving a gap between the theoretically-justified direct multiplicative method and the practically-relevant FFT alternative discussed in Section 5.

The reduction from general k-out-of-t to k=1 composition (Lemma 2.8, from prior work) is acknowledged as lossy, particularly when t/k is small (Fig. 11 shows visible gaps for large k relative to t), so the paper's tightness claims are strongest primarily in the k=1 regime.

Numerical stability limitations are noted only qualitatively (float64 breaks down below ~1e-15, requiring float128 with added cost) without a rigorous treatment of how this interacts with the paper's own tightness guarantees in extreme small-delta, high-composition regimes (e.g., the PREAMBLE experiment mentions "heavy computation load" and needing 1e6 bins, suggesting practical scalability concerns are non-trivial in the most demanding settings).
